AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Gordon for the second reading of Bill No. C-91, to amend the Income Tax Act.

Mr. Speaker, I do wish there were more members present on the government benches to hear the solid words of wisdom I am about to utter. However, I suppose their absence is understandable. Unfortunately the attitude of the government has been one of not paying too much attention to the opposition. I do not have too many remarks to make concerning Bill No. C-91. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) dealt with the principle of the bill this afternoon very adequately and at some length. I propose to
Income Tax Act
be reasonably brief but I believe there are some things that should be said at this stage.
When we get to the committee stage it will be necessary to examine many of the clauses of the bill in great detail and I say this for many reasons. To use the words of one speaker this afternoon he said, if I am correct, that it took a man of law to understand the Income Tax Act, and I assume he also meant the amendments now before us. He said that it was discriminatory and confused. I agree completely and wholeheartedly with that statement. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, the same hon. member said some things this afternoon with which I did not agree, but with that particular portion of his speech I must agree because it is so completely and absolutely true.
I have spent several hours studying the amendments, and their application to the act as it existed after the amendments of 1963. I am afraid I spent most of the time checking cross-references and so forth. To me the Income Tax Act has become almost completely impossible to understand for anybody but-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: A chartered accountant.

No, not even a chartered accountant. I doubt whether the minister knows too much about the act and its application. This is my point. I had been going to ask the minister earlier if he had received many representations from individuals, corporations, associations, organizations and what have you, concerning the terms of Bill C-91. I had intended to do so prior to second reading, but in his opening statement on second reading he said there had been and that there had been some consequential amendments. I wonder whether enough of the suggestions that may have been made in the interval since the bill received first reading have been listened to.
At the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) the minister outlined this afternoon the amendments he proposes to make as we progress through the committee stage. I have no quarrel with the amendments he has suggested will be presented, and which will undoubtedly be accepted, but I am wondering whether he has gone far enough. He referred to two amendments to delete references to family allowances. The minister suggested that as a result of the debate on the resolution stage the house seemed to be of a mind that the family allowance amendments, certain fiscal arrangements with the province of Quebec which are necessary, and the matter of income tax application should be taken up later and at one time. I agree with this step, because taking them up in a disjointed way does not

Income Tax Act
give one the whole picture of the application of each segment of the suggested extension of family allowances. I hope when the minister closes the debate he will intimate just when he contemplates the additional family allowances suggested in the budget speech will be effective. I think it is very important that we should know this.
I know there are amendments to the act, or there were, that will have the effect of adjusting exemptions for people receiving family allowances for part of this year, and that sort of thing. However, I am interested in the three categories the minister mentioned which were going to be brought in together at some future date. I am assuming that this entails amendments to the Family Allowances Act and whatever other legislation might be necessary to bring about the abatement for the province of Quebec. I am wondering when he is going to introduce these measures, and also when the family allowances are actually going to have effect. When are the people with children in school going to be able to receive these additional allowances?
The minister mentioned also that there were some further representations which were going to be given study between now and next year. I think the minister might well take a leaf out of his own book and go back to what happened to the budget of 1963. I am not going into past history, but we all remember distinctly that there were retractions, modifications and changes all the way along the line. Are we simply going to take these representations that have been made since Bill No. C-91 reached the floor of the house and deal with them at some future date? I feel we should give very close attention to all of these things at this time.
Earlier I intimated I had spent several hours studying Bill No. C-91 and the application of these amendments to the present act. At one time both the minister and I made our livelihood as practising chartered accountants. I ask him today, in all frankness, could he go back to practice as a chartered accountant today and interpret this act so he could advise clients exactly what they should do, without having to charge the clients an unholy amount of money? I do not think I could, and if the minister could he is brighter than I am.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What do you call "unholy"?

I said an unholy amount of money. My point is that this act has become so complicated that neither a chartered accountant nor some of these lawyers we have in this house could understand the act without giving it so much attention that it would make it almost prohibitive for a client to ask us to interpret the act.
If you had two lawyers, they would be on opposite sides.

As I said, I doubt if I could go back to practising today and do an honest job for a client at a reasonable fee. As a matter of fact this act is getting completely out of hand.
I did mention earlier, I believe, that I would not deal with any specific provision in the bill. However I believe there is one point that I might mention. I am going to refer to the item having to do with research. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) mentioned this this afternoon. I recall an experience of my own during my term as minister of national health and welfare. We tried to encourage pharmaceutical firms to do their research in Canada. I admit that very few did. However, these new amendments will encourage firms to have their research done at a head office in the United States, or wherever it may be. I believe we should examine this provision very closely at the committee stage.
I should like to refer to an article in the Globe and Mail of May 6, 1964. This article was written by one Ronald Anderson and he is quoting Stuart D. Thom of the Toronto legal firm of Osier, Hoskin and Harcourt. I could not be more wholeheartedly in agreement with what Mr. Thom has had to say in this article, in many respects. He says that the language of Bill No. C-91 has become "tortured and involved." I think those words describe it very well. This has been done in the hope of plugging all possible loopholes, and it will take weeks to trace all its implications. This is my concern. Anything to do with income tax does seem to take longer and longer. I am sure the layman would not have a hope if he were trying to study the Income Tax Act with any idea of ascertaining how it might affect his business. Mr. Thom says that-
*-the government has been unwilling to trust the courts to interpret general terms.
The minister has gone overboard in tinkering in an effort to try to plug up all the loopholes. I am not in favour of taxpayers getting away with anything. I have had to fight some taxpayers in the past who have attempted to get away with things. I am not in favour of that.
I do believe there is some way this act could be revised at this stage. I believe the last complete revision was in 1949. At that time we thought we had a simplification put in front of us. Since then it has grown like Topsy. I will mention one section, section 139, and say that if anyone without experience tries to trace his way through all the

consequences and cross references connected with this section he will be completely lost.
I like this particular term used by Mr. Thom. He goes on to say that the minister has attempted to define each term in specific gobbledegook. I believe that is self-explanatory. He says that the draftsmen have dug themselves deeper and deeper into something. This is my chief concern, Mr. Speaker, the whole business of the Income Tax Act and these amendments, how they will affect the act and so on. I think we are getting this legislation into such form that nobody really knows how discriminatory it might be.
He also mentions section 23 of the act, and we will be coming to that in due course. Mr. Thom mentions, in connection with trusts in which all beneficiaries must be residents of Canada, that it would be impossible in the case of any long-standing trust to apply this test. This is only an example of what people who are practitioners think of the clause in this bill and of the application of the act as a whole. Possibly this is a rather strong term, but he also adds:
I hope the idiocy of this section will be recognized before the bill is passed.
Incidentally, there is another article here. I do not believe it is by Ronald Anderson but it may be. It is entitled, "Banana-Republic Image Laid to Gordon Policies," and it gives a statement by Mr. A. G. Davies, taxation controller of the Rio Tinto-Zinc Corporation. He says:
Finance Minister Walter Gordon's attempts to put curbs on foreign investment have caused some foreign commentators to class Canada among the banana republics.
This is what he told the international corporate tax conference, and he added:
There are plenty of people in England, France and other countries who are extremely sceptical of the role of foreign capital in their economies-
But he goes on to point out that the rules should be made clear before the foreign investment comes in, so that those who provide it would know what they were doing.
The rules should not be changed in midstream, as the minister attempted to do in his budget of a year ago; and unfortunately he has not completely retracted in this budget. Rather than discriminate against foreign investment I believe there should be incentives for Canadian investment in Canadian securities.
Mr. Speaker, I said I would be brief, and I shall be. I would like simply to summarize my own conclusions concerning the minister's approach to the Income Tax Act and how it applies to Canada. I think the minister loves to tinker. He has indicated he is trying to do a tidying up job. That is fine. Tidying
Income Tax Act
up to a degree is acceptable, but I still think he is preserving all the last vestiges of discrimination that he can. I hope and pray he will soon cease trifling and tinkering with the laws which have so much to do with the welfare of our citizens. To me this approach is simply not understandable, and I hope before another year passes, in fact even before we conclude the debate on the committee stage of this bill, the minister will have some change of heart.

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised at the minister being in such a hurry, because it seems to me he loves the limelight and he could have had it all to himself for eight or nine minutes tonight before some of his colleagues came in to back him up. Therefore I hope he will not mind staying in it for a bit longer. He has more support now and should do very well.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Where are your colleagues?

I don't need any when I am speaking; I am getting along fine. I do not want to take up the time of the house just to delay this bill, but it is one that has to do with principles concerning income tax, and with perhaps a wider scope of general principles that concern taxation as a whole.
The statements made by the speaker who preceded me had a lot of merit because people across the country are becoming convinced more and more that rather than having a new era, under a new minister who has seen a new light, we are simply having a practising tinker. This word gobbledygook I think is very applicable. Those people who paid tribute to the minister and built up the stature he seemed to enjoy before he came into the house, did it on the basis of a book he wrote, but in the light of the practices he is following today it seems to me that book was a bunch of gobbledygook, and it is no surprise that this term is being applied to the bill which he has presented to the house.
In his short term in office he has tinkered with so many features of the economic field in Canada that nobody really knows in which direction we are going. I am not one of those who have great concern about friendly foreign investment in Canada. The efforts the minister made in that direction were pretty terrible, and it will take us a long time to overcome the results.
I would be far more receptive to the minister and his policies if he showed some concern about the thieving inflation that is taking place in the country. The cost of living continues to jump, and I notice that the report we got today from the dominion bureau of statistics shows it is going up and up across the country. The answer the Prime

Income Tax Act
Minister (Mr. Pearson) gave yesterday to a question about the rising cost of living, that certainly there would be inflation in this buoyant economy of ours, did not reassure anybody, especially when one considers that there are still over 400,000 unemployed in the country.
I see a misdirection in some of the policies he put forward and in some of the things contained in the general income tax measures being brought before the house. Much of what I had in mind to say on this subject has already been said, and therefore I do not believe it will carry any more weight by repetition, but in case I am not here when we come to deal with certain of the clauses in the bill I wish to pose a question which I hope the minister can answer. It has to do with provincial income tax.
As I understand it, a resident pays income tax on the basis of his residence as of December 31. It has been brought to my attention that there are differences in the provincial income taxes, in some provinces the surtax charge being 17 per cent and in others 23 per cent. Even though a man might have earned eleven twelfths of his income in one province where the 17 per cent is applicable, if he is living in another province on December 31 where the 23 per cent is applicable, he has to pay the 23 per cent on his total earnings for the year. To me this is not right. I suppose it works both ways, but I still think it is an imposition on many individuals.
When a man reports that he has earned eleven twelfths of his income in a province where the 17 per cent applies, and only one twelfth in a province where the 23 per cent applies, I am wondering why he cannot pay the 17 per cent on the eleven twelfths he earned in the first province, and the 23 per cent on the remaining one twelfth?
I was not bright enough to do this. I paid the 23 per cent. I do not quarrel about it, because I live in the most wonderful province in Canada. If we did not have so many laws made down here placing us in a discriminatory position we would have a flowering economy, but I hasten to add that, despite what happened there recently, it will continue to flower in Saskatchewan.
I would like the minister to explain why a man has to pay 23 per cent on his total earnings, if eleven twelfths of them, or ten twelfths were earned in a province where there is only a 17 per cent charge. Why should discrimination of this sort continue to exist? To an average taxpayer, $46 represents a considerable amount. I would be obliged if the minister would turn his attention to this problem.

Mr. Speaker, while we are discussing Bill No. C-91, an act to amend the Income Tax Act, I should like to expound a few ideas which, I am sure, should hold the attention of all members. We are living in an economic structure which is strangling the Canadian taxpayer at whatever financial level he may find himself.
I should like to begin by giving the house some statistics concerning the revenue of the Canadian government from taxes of all kinds, for the fiscal year 1962-63.
For instance, the general sales tax brought in the sum of $1,044,557,000; the tax on alcoholic beverages, $206,277,000; the tax on tobacco contributed $367,386,000 to the national revenue. The tax on automobiles yielded $25,270,000, the estate tax, $84,579,000-
Dispense.

Other taxes combined
brought in some $25 million in revenue.
What do those figures indicate? To a lesser or greater degree, each of those taxes is paid by the consumer, the individual.
Let us now compare the amount of taxes paid by companies, on the one hand, and private individuals, on the other. In 1962-63, companies contributed $1,302,179,000 to the federal treasury, as against $2,051,606,000 for individuals. In other words, individual taxpayers have paid $749,427,000 more than the companies.
Now take indirect taxes and add them to the figures I just gave you; you will see that, proportionally, Canadian taxpayers paid in taxes almost twice as much as the corporations. On the other hand, corporations' profits increased, always proportionally, much more than private income. Evidence that the standard of living is decreasing as far as collectable taxes are concerned is that the Minister of National Health and Welfare had to increase her department's budget by more than a billion dollars this year.
On the other hand, in Quebec, 9 per cent of the population are unemployed whereas, in 1962, the unemployed made up 6 per cent of the labour force; in mid-January this year, 466,000 people were out of work in Canada, that is 7 per cent of the labour force, and needless to say that taxable income, under the terms of the Income Tax Act, is decreasing.
And as budgets increase, taxes in the present situation do not decrease; and it is the workers who, already overburdened, have to take in the increases through government surcharges, at all levels of government, federal, provincial or municipal.

In addition, whoever considers carefully the legislation introduced in any Canadian province, as well as in this house, will readily realize that generally, companies and corporations are getting the most out of them. These companies may be the backbone of the Canadian economic structure but no need to say that the individuals are its blood and that a transfusion will soon be necessary. If the Canadian government is its nervous system then it should give the required impetus.
What is important, therefore, is to legislate with the people in mind and to fully review our position with regard to them.
The family is the basis of our society. It is therefore to the family that the greatest advantages should be granted. Let us take the head of family in the first place. Since everything nowadays is based on interest, from the financial point of view, I suggest that the government should pay interest on taxes collected from taxpayers. This would encourage people to file their income tax return, while reviving the purchasing power, and it would also help to cover, through the additional amounts collected, the administration costs and part of the interest.
I also advocate that the exemptions be increased to $3,000 for single persons and $5,000 for married people and also that a 10 per cent exemption be granted for charitable donations.
We, members of the house, seem to forget that 55 per cent of taxpayers do not earn $4,000 a year and that 34 per cent earn less than $3,000. Therefore, the number of those who pay taxes is rather small compared to the total number of Canadian taxpayers.
This 34 per cent of 4J million persons represents approximately one million and a half, and if we add to this figure the two million people who paid no income tax at all, if we add their wives and children, unemployed, old age pensioners, disabled persons, widows, small farmers, fishermen with a very low income, there is no doubt that a revision is called for.
We believe that tax cuts should benefit lower and average income groups, who would use this artificial supplement to buy consumer goods and thus help indirectly to maintain a balanced economy.
I wish to make it clear that my suggestion to pay an interest, in the present context of the financial system, is not what the Social Credit party advocates. What we advocate is to give more freedom, to give all the necessary initiative, so that everyone, either at the level of the individual or of the corporations, will be able to develop. According to Social Credit technique, taxation would apply only to capital surplus which are prejudicial to the public weal, by balancing the volume
Income Tax Act
of money and the volume of production. By a dividend originating from the Bank of Canada, the present balance of the gross national product, which is not consumed, would go into the economy, would be distributed, either by a discount offset by a drop in prices or by the dividend as outlined a moment ago. Then, we would not have to overburden individuals or companies, as long as they do not hinder the collectivity. The purchasing power enjoyed by each individual would ensure a sounder administration, quickly remove accumulated debts, give us all kinds of controls and, for once, permit all Canadians to work freely for the development of their country.
Also, the government should insist on the fact that family allowances be paid, even in Quebec, for children 16 or 17 years old, on the basis used previously. It would be up to the Quebec government to increase those allowances in the case of older students. No matter whether it is a joint program or not, we must first think of the welfare of the people; that is our primary duty.
On several occasions, attempts were made to put old age pensions in line with the cost of living. It is also important to adjust family allowances to the cost of living. The government can afford it.
If you consider that at the end of April 1963, therefore a year ago the stocks listed on the stock exchanges were valued at $54,837,791,829 and that a month earlier, they were valued at $52,503,742,402, it goes without saying that the increase of $2 billion was profitable to the companies.
Our financial organization should provide for a participation of the people, to various extents, to any economic growth, whether it comes from the government or private enterprise.
Corporations do not pay succession duties. They are taxed only after reserves and depreciation. They have therefore considerable more advantages over the individuals.
It is essential that the government introduce legislation which looks after the interest of the people in the first place. And if they do not want to cut down taxes, as in the United States, they should at least make sure that there is a fair redistribution or that the whole community pays equal taxes on a proportional basis.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I should caution the house that if the minister speaks now he will close the debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall try to deal with some of the points which were raised.

Income Tax Act
If I do not deal with them all I hope hon. members will realize they will be dealt with when we come to the respective clauses in the committee stage. I have already suggested to the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) that some of the points he brought up can, I think, better be dealt with by me when we come to the committee stage.
With regard to some of the points of principle which were brought up, it was proposed that the Income Tax Act should provide for deductions from income of union dues, workmen's tools and equipment, particularly in the case of loggers, farmers' equipment, and all other forms of expenditure which are necessarily paid out in order to earn income. I agree that this is a question of principle and an important one. It is a difficult one to deal with on an individual basis or on an item by item basis. It is a very complex question, difficult to determine, and it is my hope that it will be one of the important subjects with which the royal commission on taxation deals carefully, with the benefit of their research staff. I am rather inclined to think that if we tried to deal with it ourselves hurriedly we would find that we might solve one or two particular situations, but that others would remain to be dealt with. Therefore I would prefer to deal with these various questions, and others like them, in a more general way after receiving the report of the royal commission.
On the question of charitable donations I think I stated in the budget speech, and I think I may have mentioned it again during the resolution stage, that the government has given a lot of attention to the very difficult and irritating problem which several hon. members have mentioned. However, with the staff at our disposal, we were unable to come up with a solution which we thought would be satisfactory, and therefore the late Mr. Garland, the former minister of national revenue, with the approval of the government and after discussions with myself as Minister of Finance, referred the matter to the royal commission and asked them to give it their attention and the attention of their research staff. That is being done.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) raised the question whether contributions to political parties should be allowed as a deduction for income tax purposes. This is an intriguing idea, Mr. Speaker, but I am not sure whether it is a good one. However, I certainly find it intriguing.
Ask Mr. Davey.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understand there is a bill on the order paper which advances this suggestion and I think we might leave it until that bill comes up for debate.

Several hon. members referred to the fact that the Income Tax Act is very complex and difficult to understand. This is a complaint which I certainly share. I think it is extremely difficult. However, I would remind hon. members that with every exception which we add, with every change that we make, and with the implementation of each good idea suggested by hon. members, the act becomes just that much more complex. You can single out any section of the act and say it is more complex than some of the others; but the truth of the matter is that as a whole it is a very complex and difficult piece of legislation.
When we are faced next year with the extremely difficult task of rewriting the tax laws of this country, following upon the royal commission report, I do not know whether we will be any more successful than some of our predecessors in producing a simple, workmanlike, understandable piece of legislation. I hope we succeed; but I think we all know that income tax legislation in other countries is also very difficult and complex. While it is a good thing, I think, to remind ourselves as often as we reasonably can of the increasing complexity of these matters-it is probably good for our souls to have this fact rubbed in now and again- and while I think we should continue to strive for simplicity, I fancy that we will find next year when we are drafting new tax legislation that this is easier said than done. I say that because it is very easy to make funny remarks about the complexity of the drafting of the Income Tax Act.
The hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) referred to a friend of mine, Stuart Thom, who rather delights in making remarks about how difficult the Income Tax Act is to understand. I might say that Mr. Thom is an excellent tax lawyer; I used to retain him myself at one time when I was operating in another sphere. I would remind hon. members-and perhaps Mr. Thom will also be reading Hansard-
I wonder.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-that I have on occasion invited anyone who felt so inclined, and practically all the practitioners in the income tax field, to make suggestions for meeting the stated objectives of the government in various fields in simple language which would not be full of loopholes. I do not remember having received any constructive suggestions from my hon. friend's friend, Stuart Thom. I have received, since issuing this invitation, many suggestions from many lawyers and

accountants who practise in the field of taxation, and their suggestions have been included in some of the amendments that are now incorporated in this bill.
I imagine the minister means *"some" of their suggestions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am referring to their constructive suggestions. Those who just said, "Don't do anything" or, "Don't do anything you set out to do" I have not taken too seriously. As I think by this time some hon. members may realize, it is my hope and it is the objective of this government to see that Canadians gradually acquire a greater share of the resources, the assets and the equities of this country. We believe this will be a good thing. We do not think it can be done without a certain amount of controversy; we do not think it can be done easily, but I can assure my hon. friend that we are not going to be deterred from that objective.
No matter what the penalties are on foreign capital.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there seems to be a little off-stage noise from my friend the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith).
I admit that I did not stand up to make my statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
However, Mr. Speaker, there are not any penalties that I know of. I do not know whether I would be out of order if I referred to the question that was asked me about the extension of family allowances. I think an hon. member raised the question as to when this particular piece of proposed legislation would become effective. I can assure my hon. friend that, while it is not incorporated in this bill and therefore perhaps it is not appropriate to deal with it, the government has every intention of proceeding with this legislation just as fast as we can. I think if he and other hon. members will wait until tomorrow, perhaps the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) will have something to say about that subject.
That is perhaps all I need say at this stage, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps when we go into committee other hon. members will have questions that they wish to raise, and I will do my best to answer them.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 1-Legal costs.

Mr. Chairman, clause 1
deals with the classification as income of legal costs which may be awarded to a taxpayer by a court of appeal in relation to an
Income Tax Act
assessment of tax. This must be related to
clause 3, paragraph five, which appears on page four. I had some difficulty this afternoon-and I wish to thank the parliamentary secretary for his assistance in this connection-in relating the wording of the proposed amendment at line 15, paragraph (w), when in actual fact section 11(1) of the Income Tax Act prior to this year has contained a paragraph (w).
As I said this afternoon, though, I have some difficulty in understanding why there is not any clearcut indication as to just what level of fees or expenses may be incurred by a taxpayer in "instituting or prosecuting an objection to, or an appeal in relation to, an assessment of tax" under subparagraph (w) on page four. I raised a number of questions this afternoon and it is not my intention to repeat them; but I think we must understand that from an administrative point of view there must be some yardstick whereby the Minister of National Revenue will be able to measure whether or not fees are reasonable. I would hope this would not be another area of the Income Tax Act where indirectly the discretion of the Minister of National Revenue is brought into play.
After all, we do know that assessments vary in amount, and of course fees are related to the importance of the problem being taken before the taxing authorities. There are matters which have to be considered, such as the distances that have to be travelled, the number of appearances that have to be made, the calibre of counsel or the accounting firm who may be retained, or the specialist tax adviser. All these matters have to be considered. After all, Mr. Chairman, the business community of this country and all taxpayers are entitled to know, with a reasonable degree of certainty, what they may be allowed. I am not sure that on the face of what is contained in this bill there is any indication of this. There is no provision within the wording of the clauses that regulations may be promulgated in regard to this question. True enough, there are general provisions within the act for the making of regulations, but this matter has worried me considerably, because in my own profession as a lawyer I would like to be able to advise my clients that if they prosecute an appeal and are successful certain of their costs will be allowed, and I should like to know the extent to which such costs are allowed. The cost involved often determines whether a man thinks it is worth the candle to proceed with an appeal. There is no point in his spending hundreds and hundreds of dollars to save a lesser amount of tax if he has to spend a large sum of money prosecuting an appeal which may be disallowed by the Minister of

Income Tax Act
National Revenue in the administration of this clause. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I should like clarification from the minister in regard to this question.
In addition I would like to know whether this provision will be implemented with regard to reassessments of taxation for years prior to 1964. Will they have anything to do with assessments for the year 1963 which are now being worked out, or will they have relationship only to assessments in connection with the taxation year 1964? Those are the two prime questions that I put to the minister in this regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, to answer the second question first, they will apply to any expenses incurred in 1964, whether they apply to the year 1964 or prior years. As the hon. member for Edmonton West pointed out, we are dealing with an item in clause 1 that is related to another item in clause 3. The reason they are taken in this order is that it is customary in these amendments to follow the order of the act. With the consent of the committee perhaps I might be permitted to deal with the two clauses together.
The purpose of allowing expenses in connection with appeals or objections is essentially to give the smaller taxpayer the same break that most large taxpayers have anyway. In the case of many large taxpayers the fees they pay to the hon. member for Edmonton West and other tax lawyers, and to the hon. member for Perth and other tax accountants, are not always broken down and itemized according to each individual service that is performed. Frequently the annual fees that my hon. friend receives as auditor for a company may include an amount which covers all services of this kind and they are allowed as a deduction for tax purposes. Similarly, my legal friends frequently receive retainers which cover a variety of things and for the most part they are allowed as deductions and do not have to be itemized in detail.
But if smaller taxpayers, and sometimes a large one, feel they have not been treated fairly by the income tax authorities and want to appeal they may be in a position where they are afraid it will cost them a lot of money in the form of fees to carry through an appeal, and that the expenses in the form of the fees they incur will not be allowed as a deduction against their income. I think all hon. members really believe that we should, wherever we can, provide for appeals. I remember that last fall some of my hon. friends opposite felt that in another section there was not sufficient provision for appealing from certain rulings. I agreed that this should be rectified and an amendment was introduced which met the wishes of my hon. friends across the aisle.

What we are trying to do here is to give taxpayers as reasonable a chance as we can to appeal assessments that in their opinion are unfair and to put all taxpayers on the same basis. In the case of large companies as I have said, I suspect that most of these fees are allowed as deductions without question. My hon. friend asked if there was going to be some sort of regulations or set of rules which would stipulate the amounts that members of his profession should charge their clients in connection with these appeals. I think that the members of the committee would hesitate before they found it necessary to lay down rules as to what the fair charges should be by a taxpayer's advisers in the field of taxation. By and large I think most lawyers and most accountants who succeed over the years try to charge what they think is a fair fee for services rendered. If they charge too much the chances are they will lose the client or the client will refuse to pay.
I would remind my hon. friend that the taxpayer has a real sanction over the amount of the fees that he is going to pay. It is he who has to pay them. It is true that under the proposed amendment he will be allowed to deduct those fees from his taxable income but if he is in the 50 per cent bracket, for instance, he still has to pay half the fees. When I was in practice I did not find many taxpayers who were prepared to pay me more than I was worth just for the good of my health. I think this will be a pretty good check.
I would also remind my hon. friend that if the income tax authorities felt in any particular case that any expense, including any legal or accounting fee, was unreasonable they could invoke section 12(2) of the act which provides that in computing income no deduction shall be made in respect of an outlay or expense otherwise deductible except to the extent that the outlay or expense was reasonable in the circumstances. That is not a new section. It is there now and it gives the Minister of National Revenue discretion to disallow any expense, including any fee, that he may consider was not reasonable in the circumstances. Presumably if he disallowed some legal fee the taxpayer might appeal again, but that is his right and I think it is a good right to retain.
To come back to clause 1, if under this amendment a taxpayer is allowed to deduct from his taxable income any fees that he may pay in connection with an appeal, it is only reasonable that if he is awarded what are known as costs by the court those costs should be included in his income. Otherwise he would be getting a double break. While I am sorry for taxpayers as a rule I think we have got to be reasonable about this thing,

and he should only get one break and not a double break. That is the purpose of clause 1 in providing that any recoveries in this way should be brought back into income.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 2-Compensation by Federal Republic of Germany.

Mr. Chairman, has the minister any estimate of the extent of the payments or indemnities that may be received in this regard? I ask purely for purposes of information. I think every member of the house is in sympathy with the aim of the amendment, but is there any extensive payment under this plan or does it simply involve a relatively isolated number of cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are almost certain it is just a relatively small number of cases where there has been a feeling of injustice. These people were victims of persecution. They are being paid a small amount as compensation for that persecution, if it is possible to measure persecution in terms of a monetary payment, and it was felt they should not be taxed on it. But as far as we know it would not apply to very many people.

Mr. Chairman, I agree entirely with what the minister has said. This provision is to apply to 1960 and subsequent taxation years. Were there any such payments in prior years? Has any attempt been made to tax them in prior years? Why is this being brought forward at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My understanding is that there have been representations on this point for some time. There may have been some cases prior to 1960 where they were taxed. As my hon. friend knows, under the act it is not possible to go back more than four years. In some cases the records are not available, and that is why 1960 was taken.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the Minister of Finance what group exerted pressures or made representations to him to have this clause inserted in the act. Was it a special, well-defined group, a racial or social one? Was it an imposing group? Could the minister give us some indication of the number of Canadians affected by the amendment and the approximate amount of income that has entered Canada and will be protected by this amendment to the Income Tax Act?
I seem to detect here a very special intention to have a very particular group benefit therefrom. I have no preconceived idea against anybody, but I would really like to know how did a group of individuals succeed in
Income Tax Act
having amendments brought to the Income Tax Act in order to protect them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this group would include people who came from Germany to Canada and who, prior to or during the war, were persecuted in Germany. Following the war, the courts awarded them compensation in the form of certain capital sums. In some cases, they were awarded lump sum payments which have not been taxed, and in other cases instead of lump sum payments the amount was paid over a period of years. These representations were made to the department by certain individuals and also on behalf of other groups by the Canadian Jewish congress.

I appreciate that the minister does not have all the figures at hand, but could be give some indication of the number of people who will be affected by the amendment and of the amount involved? Would it be $100 million, $100, $200 or $200,000? He must certainly have some idea of the amount and I am sure that, with the help of his assistants, he can give us that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would judge somewhere between 100 and 200 people. I am not in a position to make a guess as to the amount, but it would be a modest sum. Certainly, it would not be anything like the figure my hon. friend mentions. I do not like to guess because I might be quite a bit out.

There is one explanation I should like with regard to the last phrase of this particular subparagraph. It reads:
-where no tax is payable in respect of that payment under a law of the Federal Republic of Germany that imposes an income tax.
As I interpret this phrase it means that a payment made by the Federal Republic of Germany to this particular class of people shall not be subject to tax where no tax is payable under German law. If a tax is payable under German law, then a tax would also be payable here in Canada. I do not know whether there is a tax convention between the two countries and therefore if a payment is subject to tax in Germany, then obviously it may be subject again to taxation in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a tax treaty with Germany, so if it is subjected to income tax in Germany there would be a tax credit here.

I have one brief question for the minister, and perhaps he could have his advisers give us an explanation. Subsection (2)

Income Tax Act
says that this section is applicable to the 1960 and subsequent taxation years.
The minister has already explained that.
I am sorry; I was distracted. [Translation]

Mr. Chairman, I come back again to that point because I find it is a little strange that, tor about 200 people, whatever their present social or economic status in Canada, the Income Tax Act should have been amended so that they may get benefits refused to other Canadian taxpayers.
Representations have been made here for many years by various groups which want to benefit to a greater extent from the Income Tax Act; and I notice that special consideration is given to the case of 100 or 200 people, immigrants who came to Canada. I am of the opinion that they do not deserve more than Canadians because if, on the one hand, those people are in need, they are no worse off than those who come under social assistance, like thousands of other Canadians who are dependant on it.
On the other hand, I am surprised that the minister should be willing to accept such a tax exemption which will represent a loss of revenue. Indeed, he claims that he needs more money and he refuses to grant similar advantages to other groups of Canadians who submit requests which are just as justified as those.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I could give some further explanation which may indicate that these people are not in the same class as others. These people suffered persecution in the concentration camps in Germany. They lost everything they had. This is a payment that the government of the Republic of West Germany is making to them as compensation for the loss they suffered. These payments are not coming to them in the form of income. I have felt, and I think others have felt, that it was quite improper that payments of this kind should be treated as income for tax purposes. I can assure hon. members, Mr. Chairman, that if there were a similar situation applicable to Canadians, which thank God there is not, these payments would not be treated as income.
Mr. Chairman, could the minister tell us the nationalities of the persons who were admitted to Canada since the last world war and who will get this tax exemption?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would hope most of these people are now Canadians. Most of them arrived here after the war. I am sure that most of them have received their Canadian citizenship since then.
They were Germans.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They were Germans or Poles, or other people who were caught up in these atrocities during the war and were placed in concentration camps. I dare say some of them would find difficulty in proving just where they came from, and some might be French.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 3-Employer's contribution to pension fund.

Mr. Chairman, with regard to subparagraph (i) of the amendment, there is reference to 120 days as against 60 days. I believe this afternoon the hon. member for Lambton-Kent raised the question as to why there was a distinction between payments made by an employer for his employee into a pension plan and the individual himself making a payment into a registered retirement plan. The individual is limited to 60 days. Undoubtedly, there is a valid explanation, but we would like to have it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I made inquiries, Mr. Chairman, after this point was raised during the debate on the resolution. I do not believe any representations have been received on behalf of individuals in this connection. I do not think there will be any hardship against any individual. If there is, I would be only too pleased to bring in an amendment next year. But it is desirable in the case of people who know where they stand and, so far as I know, all the individuals affected do know that they should make up their minds to file their claims within two months. I do not believe this is difficult for individuals, and I do not think it will result in any hardship.
In the case of some of the company profit sharing plans, there has been more difficulty because they have not had their books audited by the end of two months, and this is intended to meet that problem.

If this were so, Mr. Chairman, would it not be by reason of the fact that corporations are now required to file their returns by April 30, if the fiscal year is ending December 31; and I believe I am correct, as a result of last year's amendments the income tax return of a corporation whose fiscal year ends December 31 must now be filed by April 30-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I-
(Mr. Rheaume.]
All right-the payment by them. If their books are closed at the end of 120 days they are able to deal with this problem, but why was the figure of 120 days taken? Is this merely an arbitrary figure?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is just an arbitrary figure, because we received a lot of complaints that 60 days were not enough. Maybe 90 days or 150 days would be better, but I think 120 days will probably meet the problem.

I know that during the resolution stage the minister gave some explanation concerning this but I have just been reading clause 3(2) paragraphs (ii) and (iii). I am afraid I am not just up to it at this stage of the night, of appreciating the full import of this. Could the minister give a brief explanation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, the change is in the number of days.
That is the first one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I beg your pardon. I think the best thing I can do is read the explanatory note that is printed in the bill, because we took some trouble over it and 1 think it as clear as I can make it:
This amendment provides that a deduction for amounts contributed into a pension plan in respect of services rendered by an employee in previous years while he was not a contributor shall not exceed an amount equal to $1,500 times the number of years in which the employee rendered services while he was not a contributor. It also provides that an amount shall not be deducted under the subparagraphs being amended if it was deductible in the immediately preceding year under section 11(1) (u) of the act which refers to a transfer of contributions from a registered pension plan or a deferred profit sharing plan to a registered retirement savings plan or to another registered pension fund or declared profit sharing plan. This amendment also allows an employee to deduct an amount contributed to a pension plan in respect of services in past years while he was a contributor even though he may also claim a deduction in the same year in respect of services in past years while he was not a contributor.
To summarize the situation, the amendment makes three changes. It closes a loophole existing under the present wording. It provides that an amount may not be deducted twice, and it implements paragraph 8 of the income tax resolution which we discussed at the resolution stage. The maximum amount that anybody can obtain under this is $3,000.

Mr. Chairman, this clause is very long and involved, and even after reading the explanatory note on the opposite page it is not completely clear. I would like to recite a particular case to the minister and ask him how this clause would apply to it.
Income Tax Act
For example, there is an employee who has been working a number of years-20 years- for a company that has had a pension plan. Now, for some of those years while deductions for a pension plan were valid as deductions from income, naturally he used them. But then his employment was terminated and he was given a refund of what he had paid into the pension plan plus that portion of the company's contribution which, under the terms of the pension plan, were recoverable by him, and of course the income tax department deducted that portion. They took taxes to make up for that portion that was deducted from taxable income during those years when this was part of the law.
Now he has been reinstated and he has had to pay a lump sum back in, being the total amount he received from the pension plan when his employment was terminated. He was allowed to deduct the maximum of $1,500 from income tax as a contribution to a pension plan and in this case, after his employment was reinstated, the amount of his current contribution to the pension plan was subtracted from the maximum of $1,500, and that amounted to something like $1,200. The income tax department has refused to acknowledge or to make provision for the other amount over and above this $1,200. They have refused to accept this as a deduction in future years. I would like to ask the minister if amending the Income Tax Act in a case such as this will allow for the residue of the sum total he paid back to the pension plan to be carried on in future years until the total is used up?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am not in the tax practitioner business any more, and I find this a very complicated case. My suspicion is that my hon. friend's friend is in a better position than he was before, on two counts. First of all, I think this amendment will help him, and second, he will be able to pay a fee to some lawyer in an effort to help him solve this problem with the income tax department. But I cannot give a decision or ruling off the top of my head.

When we are in the process of passing amendments to the Income Tax Act, respecting contributions to pension plans, I think it would be well for us to understand what the effect of them will be. Does this allow for carrying forward the residue of payments that have been made, when the aggregate of those payments exceeds the maximum of $1,500? Does it allow him to carry the unclaimed balance forward until it is used up?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He is allowed to do that.

Income Tax Act

I have discussed briefly with the deputy chairman a little matter of procedure with regard to these clauses of the bill which are long and which deal with different subject matters. It would seem simpler to deal with them subclause by subclause. For example, clause 3 has eight subclauses dealing with unrelated matters and I think it would help if we were able to proceed with the consideration of these long clauses on that basis.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I assume that this will be the desire of members of the committee. Without, perhaps, actually carrying the different subclauses we might, for the sake of order in discussion proceed from one subclause to another.
We have finished two.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We have completed consideration of subclause 2.

On page 3, subclause 3, subparagraph (iii) deals with allowances for tuition of part-time students. I have read the remarks which the minister made on the resolution stage and I agree with him there has to be an arbitrary figure somewhere, and perhaps the figure of $25 is a suitable one. However, does the minister feel that within the terminology of the amendment he will cover all the educational groups or institutions which are frequented by part-time students? We know about institutions beyond high school level. That is in subparagraph (i). Then there are schools operated by or on behalf of Her Majesty or in the public field. After that, there are high schools or secondary schools providing courses leading to a secondary school certificate or diploma required for entrance to a college or university. Is this list exclusive, or do other establishments qualify if they meet these same conditions? What about the position of a full-time student who is attending a high school or secondary school where fees are being paid? For example, one of my sons attends a high school where tuition fees have to be paid. He is a full-time student. Presumably, under this measure, I shall have to continue to pay tuition fees. But if I read subclause 3 (iii) correctly, if he were a part-time student at this school which awards a secondary school certificate which is a prerequisite to entrance to a college or a university, I would be entitled to deduct the tuition fees. I am a little surprised at the ambit of this amendment. It had been my feeling that all tuition had to be at the post secondary school level, rather than within the high school level, so as to qualify.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That used to be the case but it would not be so under this amendment.
Therefore the part-time student has an advantage over the full-time student with regard to high school education.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This clause applies to students and obviously it would apply to a full-time student.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Has subclause 3 been dealt with?
Subclause 4? Subclause 5?
On subclause 5. This paragraph has apparently to be read in conjunction with clause one which provides for the reduction of legal costs. Is that right?
Yes.

The question I should like to ask is this: Is there any chance that under this amendment a taxpayer can claim twice? This new paragraph provides that the amount paid by a taxpayer in relation to an objection to an assessment or an appeal from an assessment can be set off against tax. Suppose a taxpayer incurs $300 expenses to go to Ottawa with counsel. This money is paid. Then, after his case has been heard some weeks later, a judgment is rendered and his costs are allowed. Now we have these two amounts-the amount he has paid and the amount he was awarded by the court. What happens in such a case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The amount he paid is allowed as a deduction from his taxable income. The amount awarded by the court under the heading of costs is included in his taxable income. One offsets the other.
Would that include accountant's fees as well as legal fees, and does it also include travelling expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Is there any limit to the amount which may be claimed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

The way this reads, unless I am all mixed up, which is quite possible, is that the costs awarded by the court may be deducted for tax purposes in addition to the amount that is paid, which may also be deducted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I can help the hon. member. I gave an explanation of this matter when we were discussing clause 1 but if the hon. member was not here he would not have heard it. However, I will willingly repeat it. I will have to begin with clause 3(5). Under the provision there set out, a

taxpayer is entitled to deduct from his taxable income the expenses he has to meet in the form of fees paid to his lawyer or his accountant, and those other expenses incidental to filing an appeal from or objection to an assessment. Those expenses are deductible in the year in which they are incurred. If, following an appeal, the court awards costs-I gather this legal expression means he is reimbursed by the court or by the crown for part of his expenses-the part he gets back will not be considered as free of tax, because he has already been allowed to claim those expenses as a deduction. They are regarded as taxable income.
Can the minister point out the place where that is stated in the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Clause 3(5) refers to subsection 1 of section 11 of the act, which sets out the items which can be deducted in computing the taxable income, which include -and then comes the new paragraph (w), which reads-
-amounts paid by the taxpayer In the year in respect of fees or expenses incurred in preparing... an appeal-
That is where that item would come in the act. If the hon. member refers back to clause 1, reference is made to section 6, which is the section of the act which specifies the items which must be included in taxable income and which will now include these amounts which are recovered through awards of the court.

Just one brief question. I suppose in the case of a lawyer or accountant, if either one ever gets to paying any tax, and he takes an appeal or an objection, the use of the words "amounts paid" would preclude a lawyer or accountant from being able to claim an exemption under this clause 3(5); am I correct in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think so. After all, if a lawyer or an accountant, instead of working for a client and earning income, takes a few days off to fight his own claim, that is his privilege.

In view of what the minister has said tonight in connection with section 5 and the related section 1, I think we are passing some legislation here which is not necessary. I think this piece of legislation is going to jam up our courts of appeal. There are already more appeals and objections being filed than the department can handle, and we are now going to make it possible for those appealing to have their costs paid, and there is no limit on the costs. This is a real bonanza for the lawyers and others in the profession. I think we are in-
Income Tax Act
troducing legislation here which is not necessary and that in a year or two we will be sorry it was ever put on the books.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I should make the speech I made earlier on clause 1 when some of my hon. friends were not here.
I heard it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then if it was not convincing I see no point in repeating it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we now move on to subclause 6?

Subclause 6 is related to clause 6 of the amended act. I find the principle rather startling. I should like the minister to correct me, but I think that in accepting this amendment we are accepting the principle that there can be a loss in the disposition of a capital asset in the nature of a depreciable property. For example, suppose I own a house which I have rented or I own an apartment block which I have rented, and which is subject to depreciation. It is still a capital asset. Then I sell it with either a mortgage back or on the basis of an agreement for sale. Then a year or two later I need some cash so I am prepared to sacrifice this mortgage or agreement for sale at a discount. To the extent that the proceeds of this mortgage or this agreement for sale are less than the face value of this contract of mortgage or agreement for sale, I am entitled to claim that loss, which is a capital loss, as a deduction from income.
To me, Mr. Chairman, this is a departure, because if, on the other hand, I hold another capital asset on which I suffer a loss on disposition, I am not entitled to deduct the loss from income in that taxation year; I am given the contra-privilege- that if I sell it at a profit I am not charged income on the excess. It may be that I misunderstand the principle underlying this amendment, but I should certainly appreciate getting from the minister the rationale. I realize this will also be related to clause 6, because I think clause 6 is a related amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: First of all, Mr. Chairman, dealing with the principle of the paragraph itself which is amending the section, if a taxpayer has a depreciable property and he sells it for more than its written down value, he pays tax on it.
On the recapture.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If he sells it for less than its written down value then he can claim the loss against his other income if it is the only asset in that particular class for depreciation purposes. This is the law as it stands. All that this amendment does is to extend the

Income Tax Act
section to include agreements for sale and put them on all fours with mortgages or hypothecs relating to land.

Am I correct in my re-examination of this matter that the sale refers not to the disposition of the mortgage or the agreement for sale at a discount but to the actual sale of the property in the initial instance at a figure below the depreciated value of the capital asset?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is just one more step here. If it is a depreciable property and a man sells it under an agreement for sale for $10,000, this gives him a profit over and above the written down value of, say, $2,000, so he pays tax on that.
On the $2,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. Now, if he subsequently does not collect the $10,000 under the agreement for sale-say he only gets $7,000 for it -he can then recover the $3,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we go on to subclause 7?
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we go on to subclause 8?
Carried.

Clause 4 agreed to.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS  QUEBEC- FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN PROVINCIAL STUDY OF INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question was: I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he is considering taking any immediate public position with regard to the official endeavour of the Quebec legislature in studying factors relating to the separation of Quebec from Canada? We remember well, Mr. Speaker, that as the propaganda build-up reached its crescendo before the last election the Liberal party claimed two points above most others. First, they had a leader who would lead, not procrastinate, who would make decisions, not postpone them. Second, aside from other inherited virtues such as administrative genius, the Liberal party through history and in present support was the chosen vehicle, probably by act of God himself, to bind the French and English speaking people of Canada together.
I remember in the last campaign an article beneath a picture in the Toronto Liberal twinkle explaining the significance of the affable platform togetherness of Mike and Jean. What a "combo". At last a man and party in Ottawa to match and understand the new Liberal hero in Quebec. At last someone who really understood the aspirations of Quebec.
We have had that party and that leader for 14 months. I ask any member of the house to answer this fairly: Have the relations between French Canada as represented by Quebec and English speaking Canada improved? Of course they have not. The responsibility for the drift, the indecision, the wavering, the howeverish, maybeish, on the otherhandish approach is, it seems to me, the inanition of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson).
If anyone in English speaking Canada comments unfavourably on this or on the quiet revolution and its course, he is labelled as destructive and as an English speaking separatist. The Prime Minister perambulates saying that English speaking Canada must realize that if we lose Quebec we will slip down the slope into the United States. It would seem to me that the new dispensation this government has given us overlooks the
3294	HOUSE OF
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion national spirit and loyalty to a Canadian concept of English speaking Canada in its apparent willingness, if you follow the cliches of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau), to decentralize. Quebec, they say, and many of us agree, is not a province like the others. Then they go on to glorify and support a decentralization that must destroy the Canada that many of us thought we had. It is the Prime Minister and no one else who has the policy that will fragment Canada and lead to American absorption.
The question raised in the house is a case in point. What a reflection, when you think of it, that it had to be asked. Can you imagine presidents Kennedy or Johnson or even Eisenhower remaining mute at the decision of a state in the American federation through its state legislature to study and report on the separation of that state from the union?
The situation revealed by the Quebec legislature's intention is covered very well in the discursive report in yesterday's Montreal Star. Listen to it and you will see why I ask the question and why it never should have had to be asked, why the Prime Minister should have given a statement on the attitude of the government toward this intention. I am not suggesting for a moment that the Quebec legislature should not go ahead with this kind of study, but surely I as a citizen of Canada should not feel that I may have to turn to the premier of Ontario to get someone who will go into Quebec, deal with these people and see if we cannot turn aside from the direction in which we seem to be going because the federal government cannot seem to do anything about stopping it. The story reads as follows:
On the surface, at least, nobody has any real quarrel against the study that will be undertaken in the next few weeks by a group of experts to find out what possible repercussions separatism might have on the people of Quebec.
Interviews with prominent legislature members and high civil servants showed that the move is welcome in all quarters. One member of the legislature-who asked that his name be kept secret-said he did not think the separatists themselves would be "angry" because the government is actually "recognizing a fact of life".
He added that the group of experts-still to be appointed-will, in fact, feel the pulse of the population and report on the real implications that would face the people should Quebec secede from confederation.
The Prime Minister has told us that he does not intend to preside over the dissolution of Canada. I suggest that it is about time he took a more positive stand than his present lack of any comment on this matter would seem to indicate.
Yesterday, the parliamentary committee on the constitution decided to ask a number of specialists to try to find out what "possible repercussions the


independence of Quebec would have on the economic, political, social and cultural realities of the problem."
I suggest there is one point that they missed in their study-what these economic, cultural and social repercussions would be on the rest of the country. It is a rather dreadful irony that at the very time the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism is peregrinating across the country, especially in English speaking Canada, asking for English speaking Canadians to consider a move toward some greater understanding that we have this particular move within the province of Quebec and no real reply to it. What an irony that these two commissions are going on at the same time.
I continue to quote from the story, Mr. Speaker:
But the main problem is not what the group of experts will find out, most sources say. Rather, it is what the committee on the constitution is ready to accept as a fact and thus recommend to the legislature.
This, they say, is the major point. No matter who takes an active part in the study on separatism, their conclusions will influence the policy of the government for years to come.
This is rather obvious, yet we do not even have a statement of the position of the federal government except from those federal cabinet ministers who go into Quebec and appeal to the people not to talk about separatism.

Cabinet ministers, on the whole, are behind the idea of a study on separatism. They say-although none of them would like to be quoted here-that they will be glad when the findings of the inquiry have been made public.
They also say a cool analysis of the "revolution in Quebec" will profit the party in power, because it will give it a tool against the opposition, already trying to woo the separatists.

Should the movement prove itself economically and emotionally profitable, a cabinet minister told me yesterday afternoon, then there would be no alternative for the government but to separate from the rest of Canada.
I just put that on the record, Mr. Speaker, to indicate what I think is the seriousness of the possible result of this study if the national government, and I assume we still have a national government, does not take some kind of public position on what contribution it is going to make to this question.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Davis (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS  QUEBEC- FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN PROVINCIAL STUDY OF INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, the position of the Prime Minister on this matter has been made abundantly clear. Separation is unthinkable. Let me quote from the Prime Minister's speech in the budget debate which appears on page 2145 of Hansard for April 14, 1964. I quote:
Every province must be in a position to exercise its right and discharge its responsibilities, and Quebec in these matters has a special position. But equally it must be accepted and established that Canada is above all the provinces, embracing all the provinces, respecting provincial division and provincial responsibility, but that Canada, as a nation, is greater than its parts or the sum of its parts. French speaking Canada must play a proud and equal part in that nation, must feel that it belongs to Canada and that Canada from sea to sea belongs to it.
Canada is a very proud name in the world today and has been over the years. Our country need not and must not become balkanized-
Farther along I read this:
We must do nothing, either by provocation or by weakness or by stubborn unawareness of the basic nature of our federalism or by words or actions based on prejudice or fear, to bring about that weakening or disappearance.
I think those quotations, Mr. Speaker, should answer the question raised by the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, a few days ago, I directed to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) a question which I would like to repeat tonight to the house:
At the request of home builders of the province of Quebec in particular, does the government intend to amend the Bankruptcy Act in order to stem the present wave of fraudulent bankruptcies in the field of housing?
May I say that French Canadians had nothing to do with 86 per cent of commercial bankruptcies in Canada and 72 per cent of those which occurred in the province of Quebec in the first quarter of 1964. This was
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion shown by the economic development council in its bulletin: Le Laissez-passer canadien-frangais.
On the other hand, if I refer to a report from the dominion bureau of statistics, here is what it says:
In 1963, there were 3,678 commercial bankruptcies in Canada (3,190 in 1962). Their total liabilities amounted to $193,771,000 ($149,440,000).
In the housing field, there were 714 bankruptcies in the total amount of $40,137,000.
Mr. Speaker, while Hon. Mr. Fulton was minister of justice, he had instituted, in 1962, I believe, an inquiry on bankruptcies. I am wondering why this government has not continued the excellent work undertaken by the minister of justice?
In my opinion, it is important and urgent- in fact nationally urgent-to amend the Bankruptcy Act so as to prevent as many frauds as possible. There are in Canada people of good faith who lose large amounts of money because the Bankruptcy Act is too vague.
Mr. Speaker, there is another important point I should like to stress concerning bankruptcies. The 11 per cent tax on building materials contributes to the financial difficulties of contractors and subcontractors. It should not be forgotten that a housebuilder's margin of profit is only 10 per cent, according to statistics; therefore, it is not surprising that bankruptcies are on the increase in Canada.
It seems to me that it is necessary and even essential to amend the Bankruptcy Act if we are to prevent as much as possible those frauds which involve great losses for private enterprise.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the question raised by the hon. member I must say I am unable to accept the premise contained in it. His question affirms that there is at present a wave of fraudulant bankruptcies in Canada, particularly in the field of housing. I have made inquiries of the officials in the Department of Justice, in particular of the officials charged with the administration of the Bankruptcy Act, and they inform me there is no evidence in the department that would support the premise alleged by the hon. member that there is a wave of bankruptcies involving fraud at the present time.
Very often we read in the newspapers and hear statements that fraud exists to a great extent in bankruptcy proceedings, but on investigation these prove to be rumours, surmises and not borne out by the facts.
We have had, of course, many representations from responsible people to the effect that
